narrative.text: Introduction: argues that LLM chatbots could change how UK public health guidance is retrieved and shared, that no benchmark covers public health or UK Government guidance, and that frequent revisions make current guidance hard for LLMs. Lists four contributions: PubHealthBench, an MCQA benchmark of over 8000 questions generated from more than 500 UKHSA documents on gov.uk (Full and a manually Reviewed subset); PubHealthBench-FreeForm, judged by a grounded LLM judge; evaluations of 24 LLMs; and a human expert review of 800 questions plus a search-engine human baseline from 5 people on 600 questions.
Heading-only block: the section number 2.1 under 'Related work', with no body text; the subsections follow as separate blocks.

Related work on MCQA evaluations: domain knowledge of LLMs has long been tested with existing human exams (e.g. the USMLE in medicine), then with broad benchmarks such as MMLU and the corrected, harder MMLU-Pro, and with domain sets such as GPQA and ARC for science. Includes the footnotes that most included guidance is English public health guidance in English only, and the GOV.UK reuse policy link, plus the caption of Figure 2 (example questions).

Related work on synthetic MCQA datasets: automated question generation grounded in corpora, including GPT-4-Turbo-generated distractors for MMLU-Pro, human-LLM pipelines for SuperGPQA and for tropical and infectious disease evaluation, and the fully automated YourBench framework for MMLU-style evaluations from new documents.

Related work on public health evaluations: clinical medicine has benchmarks but public health (prevention, environmental hazards, community interventions, outbreaks) has none. The nearest work assessed ChatGPT 3.5 on 119 UK Faculty of Public Health Diplomate exam questions, Ayers et al. on 23 questions in 4 domains, and Harris et al. on classification and extraction from guidance text. Carries the caption of Figure 3, the MCQA generation pipeline.

Methods overview: an automated pipeline (Figure 3) extracts text, chunks it into sections, generates MCQA samples and filters to a high-quality subset. Automation is chosen because manual authoring of thousands of questions is slow, guidance is revised often, and the approach extends to other knowledge bases.

Data collection: 1,150 current UK Government guidance documents in HTML and PDF were collected from gov.uk. The sources are public and probably in pre-training data, but because every question and answer option is synthetically generated, the benchmark itself cannot have been in training data.

Pre-processing and chunking: HTML is converted to markdown; PDFs go through two stages, raw text extraction with existing tools and then GPT-4o-mini vision re-extraction of each page given the page image, the raw text and the header hierarchy. Documents are split on markdown headers into 20,488 section chunks, each carrying its parent headers for context.

Question generation: an LLM first filters out chunks with no public health recommendation and chunks over about 2000 words, leaving 7,946. Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct then writes two questions per chunk, each with one correct answer and six distractors, using a one-shot chain-of-thought prompt with JSON output and the neighbouring chunks as context, giving 15,666 well-formed candidate questions.

Automated error detection and sampling: Llama-3-70B-Instruct flags potentially invalid questions, reducing 15,666 candidates to 14,440 (details in Appendix A.1). Questions from withdrawn guidance are removed and HTML and PDF sources are balanced; about 4,000 unused PDF-derived questions are kept as an internal hold-out set.

The final benchmark: PubHealthBench has 8,090 MCQA questions across public, clinical and professional guidance, 10 topic areas and 352 guidance areas, from 687 documents. Includes the captions of Figure 4 (questions by topic and audience) and Figure 5 (review steps).

Human expert quality assurance: a random sample of 800 questions (about 10%) was reviewed manually, giving an estimated 5.5% (4.1–7.3%, 95% Wilson CI) ambiguous or invalid questions. Most invalid ones had a distractor as good as the answer, so with guessing between two plausible answers the estimated upper bound on the score is about 97%.
Model evaluation approach: 24 open-weight and proprietary LLMs are assessed, including GPT-4.5, Claude-Sonnet-3.7, Gemma-3, o1, Phi-4, OLMo-2 and Llama-3.3.

The three benchmark variants: PubHealthBench-Full (the whole MCQA set, broken down by topic); PubHealthBench-Reviewed (760 expert-reviewed questions, reported with and without the ones judged invalid, and used instead of Full for the most expensive models); and PubHealthBench-FreeForm (the same reviewed questions asked without options, answers judged against the source by a grounded LLM judge).

Human baseline: non-specialist test takers answered 600 questions with search engines but no AI tools, at about 2 minutes per question, and scored 88%, roughly 9 points below the 97% upper bound. This is meant to simulate a member of the public looking up guidance quickly (Appendix A.4).

Experimental setup: prompts and answer extraction follow MMLU-Pro, but evaluation is zero-shot to resemble a chatbot query, with chain of thought only where a model does it by default (reasoning models). No model is given tools, search or document repositories.

Free-form evaluation: because each question is grounded in a source chunk, an LLM judge (GPT-4o-Mini) receives the question, the ground-truth answer, the model's response and six retrieved related chunks, and gives a binary verdict on whether the response is consistent with the source and the correct MCQA answer (Appendix A.7).

Overall MCQA results: Full and Reviewed accuracies agree closely (correlation over 0.99, rank correlation 0.98, under 1 point mean difference). Tables 1–3 give accuracy by topic area, by audience, and with and without refusals or invalid questions: GPT-4.5 leads at 92.5% overall on Full, Gemma-3-1B is lowest at 47.6%, and GPT-4.5, GPT-4.1 and o1 exceed 90% on Reviewed, above the human baseline. Most 5–15B open-weight models exceed 75%. Reasoning models (o1, o3-Mini) gain little over non-reasoning ones, and models still get about 60% of invalid questions right, supporting the ~97% upper bound.

Results by topic and audience: models do consistently better on Climate and Health and on Health Protection in Inclusion Health Settings, and worse on Chemicals and Toxicology. They know guidance for the general public best and clinical guidance least; GPT-4.5 reaches 96% on public guidance. Figure 6 shows each model's deviation from its overall score by topic and audience.

Free-form results: the setting is harder because there are no options to prompt recall or allow elimination and because models can add inconsistent information. Scores fall by up to 60 points; the best model, o1, scores 74% with the smallest drop (−17 points). Three other judges agree closely. Drops vary widely: Phi-4-14B falls over 45 points while Gemma-3-12B falls about as much as the leading proprietary models. Public guidance is again answered best.

Discussion: leading LLMs know UK public health guidance well, even though 31% of questions came from documents updated in 2024, after many training cut-offs. Free-form performance is much lower, mainly from omitting or contradicting guidance rather than adding extra advice; o1's problematic answers often concern the timing of interventions. Tables 4 and 5 give free-form accuracy by audience and the MCQA-to-free-form drop per model (from −17 for o1 to −63 for Phi-4-4B). The gap between large and small (1–15B) models widens from 10–20 points in MCQA to over 35 in free form, so small models carry real hallucination risk. Models do best on guidance for the general public, the highest-risk users of chatbots.

Limitations: MCQA and single-turn free form cover only some ways LLMs are used; multi-turn, image, adjacent-topic and tool-using queries need study. The data are English-language, openly licensed UK Government guidance that may be in training data, so results may not transfer to other countries, languages or health settings.

Conclusion: an automated pipeline produced PubHealthBench to test LLM knowledge of current UK Government public health guidance, evaluated in full, reviewed and free-form versions across 10 topics and 3 audiences. Proprietary LLMs know the guidance well, but matching it in free-form answers remains a challenge; the authors hope the benchmark supports further evaluation and safer deployment.

Ethics statement: annotators were full-time employees paid at least the minimum wage; all data came from gov.uk under the Open Government Licence 3.0 and GOV.UK reuse terms; LLMs helped generate some diagrams and figures.

Reproducibility statement and references: the full dataset and example evaluation code are supplementary material, with generation details in the paper and Appendix A.6, and the retrieved chunks given to the free-form judge are included in the dataset. The rest of the block is the reference list (Phi-4, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, HealthBench, MMLU-Pro, SuperGPQA, LLM-as-a-judge and others).
Heading-only block: 'Appendix' with the subsection number A.1 and no body text.

Appendix A.1, automated MCQA error detection: synthetic generation allows a high-recall, low-precision LLM filter. An evaluation set from an early, error-prone pipeline version was hand-annotated with five categories adapted from Gema et al. (valid; ambiguous question; ambiguous options; and others). With Llama-3-70B the binary filter would have cut the error rate from about 16% to about 8% on that set, but in the final pipeline better prompting and Llama-3.3 made the filter less critical: only about 8% of generated questions were flagged, against 44% in the early test set.

Appendix A.2, additional statistics: captions only, for Figure 8 (questions by the source document's last revision date, noting a revision may be minor) and Figure 9 (questions by source document type, and the human quality annotations, where 'Good' and 'Acceptable' count as valid).

Appendix A.3, the question-generation prompt (Table 6): the model plays a public health expert writing a test on UK guidance, focusing on material public health information and not trivia such as phone numbers. Given guidance with a highlighted passage, it lists the passage's key points, lists the context any question must carry, writes self-contained questions answerable from that passage alone with one correct answer and plausible distractors, and outputs JSON following a one-shot example.

Appendix A.4, human annotation: two annotation exercises, one estimating the rate of invalid or ambiguous questions and one setting the human baseline; all annotators were full-time staff with data science or public health experience.

Appendix A.4.1, estimating the error rate: judging question validity and when a distractor becomes an equally valid answer is subjective, so annotation ran in two rounds: 150 questions double-reviewed by pairs with disagreements resolved together, then 650 reviewed singly by the same people. Gives the reviewers' protocol, which classes questions as Good (answerable, clear best answer, non-trivial distractors), Acceptable (including easy questions or ones drawing on neighbouring text) or Invalid (unanswerable, misleading options or construction errors), with Wilson 95% intervals reported.

Appendix A.4.2, human baseline: 600 of the 800 reviewed questions, including ones judged invalid, were split among 5 test takers who had not reviewed them. Their instructions: one correct option per question, choose the answer best reflecting UKHSA guidance, guess when unsure, aim for about 2 minutes per question, use any public online resources but no LLM tools.

Appendix A.5, setup and compute: greedy decoding (temperature 0) where possible; OpenAI reasoning models at low reasoning effort; proprietary models through APIs and open-weight models served with vLLM on up to two A100 80GB GPUs each, with the same hardware for the generation pipeline; a $400 budget for proprietary evaluations including the judge.

Appendix A.6, evaluation prompts: Table 8, the zero-shot MCQA prompt, frames the model as a public health agency expert and asks for the letter of the correct answer among seven options in the form 'The answer is (X)' for UKHSA guidance on gov.uk as of 08/01/2025. Table 9, the free-form prompt, asks the same question with no options.

Appendix A.7, the free-form LLM judge: framed as binary classification of whether a response agrees with the correct answer and source text. The judge gets the source chunk, 5 more chunks retrieved by a hybrid of embedding (text-3-embedding-large) and TF-IDF similarity, and the correct MCQA option (prompt in Table 10). It was validated by inserting known correct and incorrect options into simulated chat responses; gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 with greedy decoding scored over 99% on 10,517 such samples.

Appendix A.7.1, judge comparison: the free-form evaluation was rerun with Llama-3.3-70B, MedGemma-27B and Phi-4-14B as judges besides GPT-4o-Mini; the four agree substantially (Fleiss's kappa 0.64), as Figure 10 shows.

Appendix A.7.2, error analysis: Llama-3.3-70B labels incorrect free-form answers as adding extraneous information, omitting required points, or contradicting the guidance (Figure 11). Also reproduces the judge prompt (Table 10), which requires the answer to match the ground truth without omitting key details and any extra detail to appear in the context, with a JSON verdict and reasoning.

Appendix A.7.3, problematic responses: a manual review of o1's contradicting answers found deviations that mostly recommend clinical or public health interventions too early, too late, or not at all in the guidance. Figures 12–15 show four examples beside the official passages.

Appendix A.8, confidence intervals: tables of 95% Wilson score intervals for the accuracies reported in the main results, by topic area for PubHealthBench-Full (7,929 questions, refusals counted as wrong) and for the other result tables, down to the free-form scores of the smallest models.

Title, authors and abstract: 'Healthy LLMs? Benchmarking LLM Knowledge of UK Government Public Health Information' by Joshua Harris and ten colleagues at the UK Health Security Agency. The abstract introduces PubHealthBench (over 8000 questions from 687 current UK government guidance documents, generated by an automated pipeline) and reports that GPT-4.5, GPT-4.1 and o1 exceed 90% MCQA accuracy and beat humans using cursory search, while no model scores above 75% on free-form answers, so safeguards may still be needed. Ends with the caption of Figure 1 (Full/Reviewed and FreeForm accuracy with 95% Wilson CIs).
